_releases.body:
CyteArc 1.4.0 analyzes four kinds of experiments that 1.3.0 could not: pooled CRISPR screens, clonal lineage tracing, immune repertoires, and mitochondrial and targeted DNA variants. It replaces `ds.pipeline.run` with one pipeline recipe per modality, saves diagnostics with each result so that a reused result repeats its warnings, and raises a `MemoryBudgetError` that names the budget a step needs when `mem_budget` is too small. Seven new tutorials cover the new analyses, and every tutorial was executed again and rewritten from its fresh outputs. This release merges 213 pull requests.

Read the breaking changes before upgrading: code that calls `ds.pipeline.run` needs the new recipes, several kinds of results that 1.3.0 saved are computed once more on their next call, and runs that 1.4.0 saves do not open in 1.3.0.

## Breaking changes

### Pipeline runs and example stores

- `ds.pipeline.run` is removed, with no alias. Use `ds.pipeline.rna`, which takes one keyword per stage, or the new `ds.pipeline.atac`, `ds.pipeline.adt` and `ds.pipeline.multimodal` recipes (#38). The [migration table](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/api/pipeline.html#migrate-from-pipeline-run) maps each argument, such as `hvg_count=N` to `hvg={"top_n": N}` and `params={"umap": {...}}` to `umap={...}`. Paris clustering is now off by default (pass `paris=True`), `filtering` defaults to `None`, and callbacks receive `run_interrupted` in place of `pipeline_interrupted`. Runs that `pipeline.run` saved still open and report.
- New runs cluster every Leiden resolution in one `leiden` stage and return the candidates as `run["leiden"]`, a tuple ordered by resolution, in place of one `run["leiden_<resolution>"]` per candidate (#349). Their cell tables and exports hold only the selected `clusters`. Runs saved by 1.3.0 keep their `leiden_<resolution>` names. To read a candidate the same way in runs of both releases, use `ds.artifacts.find("clusters", graph=run["connectivity_map"], method="leiden", resolution=1.0)`.
- CyteArc 1.3.0 cannot read the runs that 1.4.0 saves, because their records hold fields that 1.3.0 does not know: 1.3.0 skips them when it lists runs, raises when it opens one, and its `report()` rejects their stage records (#38, #283, #349).
- The example stores of the `cytearc_docs` CyteBase repository were rebuilt with this release and republished in place (#266, #352). Their saved runs come from the pipeline recipes, hold the diagnostics that this release checks, and return Leiden candidates as `run["leiden"]`. The tutorials of 1.3.0 open `label="docs_default"`, which these stores no longer hold, so use the tutorials of this release with them.

### Results computed again

- Results that 1.3.0 saved for highly variable genes, PCA, Harmony, neighbor graphs, UMAP, HTO demultiplexing, cell calling, ambient RNA estimates and doublet scores hold no diagnostics, so their next call computes them once more, with the same values, and the results built on them follow (#179, #190, #196). On a read-only store, such as an `hf://` dataset, that recomputation raises `PermissionError`. A call that reads such a result directly, such as `ds.reduction.harmony` on an earlier PCA or `ds.qc.correct_ambient` on an earlier estimate, raises a `ValueError` that names the call to run first. Neighbor artifacts no longer carry a `self_hit_rate` attribute; read `ds.artifacts.inspect(ref).diagnostics["selfHitRate"]` instead.
- `ds.trajectory.pseudotime` now computes the untruncated population balance potential with MINRES by default (#229). Pseudotimes, and the fate maps and lineage results built on them, shift where a graph's slow modes outnumber 30 and agree closely elsewhere, and saved pseudotimes are computed again on the next default call. Pass `method="truncated"` to reproduce 1.3.0. `n_singular_vals` and `random_seed` now apply only to that method and raise `ValueError` otherwise.
- Two fixes listed under major bug fixes change saved results: melded gene scores and fractional size factors normalize correctly (#167), and HTO demultiplexing refuses a zero cutoff where ambient tags reach the cells, so its saved calls are computed once more (#189).

### API changes

- `ds.compare.compute_bulk` returns a `BulkProfiles` record in place of a DataFrame or tuple (#228). Bulk columns are indexed by their labels, as a MultiIndex of group, subgroup and replicate, instead of joined names. `return_fraction` and `return_n_cells` are removed: pass `count_detected=True` for detection counts and fractions, and read cell counts from the record's `columns`. `ds.regulons.profiles` rows are indexed by the group labels themselves.
- `ds.trajectory.aggregation` and `cytearc.trajectory.feature_dynamics.knn_clustering` take `n_neighbors` in place of `n_neighbours`, with no alias (#351). Aggregations saved by 1.3.0 are still reused. Names, messages and plot labels now use US English.
- The PCA elbow plot numbers components from 1, so its line stands on the number to pass as `dims` (#336). Its `variance_explained` table holds `pc` in place of the 0-based `component`, and `provenance.extras["elbow_pc"]`, one higher, replaces `provenance.extras["elbow"]`.
- Flags such as `invalidate_cache`, `show` and the `transparent` argument of `PlotResult.save` accept only Python and NumPy booleans and raise `TypeError` for anything else, where 1.3.0 used the truth of any value (#137). `ds.artifacts.load` and `ds.artifacts.inspect` raise `TypeError`, not `AttributeError`, for an argument that is not an `ArtifactRef`.
- Plots title a bare label artifact from its record, such as "Leiden, resolution 1.0", in place of its kind, and an embedding keys that artifact's panel in `result.axes` by the same title (#350). The new `cytearc.plotting.NamedCellArtifact(name, artifact)` sets the title and key.
- `CategoricalScale` leaves `missing_color`, `missing_label` and `palette_name` as `None` unless set, so a scale that sets only some fields keeps a column's stored order and colors (#345).
- `ds.imputation.compute_imputed` refuses a feature name that several features share, with a `ValueError` that names their IDs, where 1.3.0 imputed their mean; `FeatureRef(value=name, reduction="mean")` asks for the mean (#223). A missing feature raises `KeyError`, and `ds.markers.load` adds a `feature_id` column.
- `Repository.download_dataset` keeps an existing `data.zarr` and the results saved in it, where 1.3.0 downloaded and replaced it (#330). A store made from an older version of the dataset raises `FileExistsError`; pass `overwrite=True` to replace it.
- Memory refusals raise `cytearc.MemoryBudgetError`, a subclass of `MemoryError` (#141, #142). A Seurat import refused by its budget raised a `ValueError` subclass in 1.3.0, so `except ValueError` no longer catches it.

### Imports and stores

- Imports detect normalized values. A non-integer matrix imported without `values=` is stored as normalized values when it fits a normalized reading, so steps that need counts refuse it, and fractional counts, such as alevin or RSEM estimates, need `values="counts"` (#165). Negative values are refused. A store that 1.3.0 imported from normalized values still reads as counts; import it again with `values=`.
- `DataStoreMerge` and `create_composite` refuse sources whose size factors differ, and an RNA assay whose stored `size_factor` is not a finite positive number no longer opens (#167).
- A pandas Categorical inserted into a cell or feature table is stored as integer codes beside its categories (#233). CyteArc 1.3.0 cannot open a store that holds such a column. Stores written by 1.3.0 open unchanged.
- Readers refuse malformed input that 1.3.0 read silently: Matrix Market entries with more fields than the header declares, a Matrix Market header that declares no entries for a file that holds some, and cisTarget motif annotation rows of another width than their header (#139, #176). `MtxReader` and `CSVReader` now detect compression from a file's first bytes rather than its name.
- `to_h5ad(nthreads=0)` raises, since `nthreads` must be at least 1 (#231).

### Memory budgets

- Budgets count only the memory that grows with the data (#159). The fixed allowances for Python, Zarr and NumPy objects, Paris's 1.35 headroom factor and Harmony's added eighth are gone, so a budget admits these steps at smaller sizes, and a process can exceed `mem_budget` by the runtime's own memory.
- Reads reserve each chunk's compressed bytes beside its decoded bytes, and the chunk a reader still holds, so a budget just above the 1.3.0 charge can now raise `MemoryBudgetError` or run fewer blocks at once (#133, #342, #347).
- On Windows, the default budget is 75% of physical memory, in place of a fixed 6 GiB (#304). Where CyteArc reads neither physical memory nor a cgroup limit, the default budget raises `RuntimeError` naming `mem_budget` and `CYTEARC_MEM_BUDGET`.

### Regulons and dependencies

- `ds.regulons.grn` and `cytearc.regulons.infer_grn` fit on spawned worker processes when `nthreads` is above 1, so a script that calls them must keep its top-level code under `if __name__ == "__main__":` (#234). Notebooks need no change.
- `cytearc.regulons.regulon_specificity` refuses labels that are missing or blank with a `ValueError`, as `ds.regulons.specificity` does (#373). In 1.3.0 a `None` label scored as a group of its own and NaN labels added rows of NaN; pass the activity and labels of the labeled cells instead.
- CyteArc requires zarr 3.4.2 or later, in place of 3.4.0, because zarr 3.4.0 held about 520 bytes per character to read a text scalar (#127).
- CyteArc requires umap-learn below 0.6, because its UMAP compiles three private functions of umap-learn that a later release could change (#269).

## New features

### Pooled CRISPR screens

The new `ds.perturbation` namespace analyzes a pooled CRISPR screen method by method, and `ds.pipeline.perturbation` runs the whole analysis as one pipeline run that checks every setting before it writes (#64, #65, #71, #85, #94).

- Call each cell's guides with `ds.perturbation.call_guides`, by a Poisson-Gaussian mixture (the default), a Gaussian, a fixed or a top-guide rule, or import Cell Ranger's calls with `import_guide_calls` (#43, #45, #46, #88).
- Label cells by the genes their guides target with `labels`, and check that each perturbation lowered its target with `efficiency` (#47, #48, #93).
- Measure how far each perturbation moves its cells from the control cells with `edistance`, scPerturb's E-distance (#49).
- Separate knocked-out cells from escapers with `signature` and `mixscape` (#59). On the 20,729 cells of the Papalexi et al. (2021) screen, `mixscape` assigns the same class as Seurat 5.5.1 to every cell in about 7.5 s on 4 threads, where Seurat's `RunMixscape` takes 10 to 14 minutes.
- Test which genes each perturbation changes with `associations`, SCEPTRE's calibrated test, for low-MOI screens and, with `moi="high"`, for high-MOI screens such as enhancer screens (#61, #72, #73, #89). On the Papalexi screen it matches sceptre 0.99.1 and runs in 126 s on 4 threads, against 829 s for serial sceptre.
- Build each perturbation's expression profile against the control cells with `profiles`, and group perturbations with similar effects with `cluster` (#63).
- The screen methods stay within the memory budgets they name (#79, #80, #91, #92, #97, #152), and their warnings come from saved diagnostics (#248).
- New figures: `ds.plots.guide_calls`, `guide_thresholds`, `efficiency`, `edistance`, `mixscape`, `association_volcano`, `association_calibration` and `perturbation_clusters` (#43, #46, #48, #49, #59, #61, #63, #178).

### Clonal analysis and lineage tracing

The new `ds.clones` namespace analyzes clones from any lineage tracing source.

- Import clone calls written by CoSpar, TREX, CellTag-multi, CellTagR, STICR, Cassiopeia, Numbat, MiTo or a Matrix Market clone matrix with `ds.clones.import_clones`, or read clones from a cell column with `from_column` (#108).
- Measure clonal expansion, diversity and rarefaction (#109, #129), compare groups by the clones they share with `overlap` and follow clones across groups with `track` (#110), and measure fate coupling and the fate bias of early cells as CoSpar does with `coupling` and `fate_bias` (#111). Results match scirpy, scRepertoire, iNEXT, immunarch and CoSpar to numerical precision.
- Import expressed lineage barcodes from eight tools with `import_barcodes`, and call clones by the published LARRY, TREX, CellTag or CellTag-multi rules with `barcode_clones` (#117, #118, #157). Diagnostics show when error correction merges unrelated barcodes.
- Import CRISPR lineage recorder alleles from DARLIN, CARLIN, Cassiopeia, PEtracer, DNA Typewriter and TreeData files with `import_alleles`, export character matrices for Cassiopeia and LAML with `export_characters` (#123), and call clones from rare alleles by DARLIN's graph rule or CARLIN's p_clonal test with `allele_clones` (#124).
- Import cell phylogenies from Newick and TreeData files with `import_phylogeny`, and cut them into clones at a time or depth with `phylogeny_clones` (#125).
- New figures, drawn through one shared chart layer whose legends `compose_results` can share: `ds.plots.clone_abundance`, `clonal_expansion`, `clonal_diversity`, `clonal_rarefaction`, `clone_overlap`, `clone_tracking`, `clone_coupling`, `clone_fate_bias`, `barcode_calls`, `recorder_states` and `phylogeny`, which draws a tree of 2.4 million nodes in under 0.4 s (#108, #109, #110, #111, #117, #123, #138, #144, #147, #156).
- The clone, repertoire and variant methods share CyteArc's argument and column names (#136, #140), count every array a call holds against its memory budget (#146, #151), and find the distinct values of large integer arrays by sorting, tens of times faster than hashing on millions of cells (#128).

### Immune repertoires

The new `ds.repertoire` namespace analyzes T cell and B cell receptors, and matches scirpy 0.25.1 cell for cell on public 10x data.

- Import Cell Ranger contig annotations or AIRR Rearrangement files with `ds.repertoire.import_receptors`, which classifies each cell's chains (#112).
- Group cells into clonotypes by identical junctions with `clonotypes` (#113), or into clonotype clusters by similar junctions with `metric` and `max_distance` (#114). On 46,526 cells, Levenshtein clusters take 0.3 s, where scirpy's `ir_dist` takes 88 s.
- Count V, D, J and C gene usage and junction lengths with `gene_usage` and `spectratype` (#115), and export AIRR Rearrangement files for Immcantation and other tools with `export_airr` (#116).
- Clonotypes defined across receptor types also record each cell's clonotype within its type, which every summary uses (#155).
- New figures: `ds.plots.receptor_qc`, `gene_usage`, `gene_pairing` and `spectratype` (#112, #115, #147, #166).

### Mitochondrial and targeted DNA variants

The new `ds.variants` namespace calls genotypes and clones from per-cell variant counts.

- Import per-cell allele counts from mgatk, maegatk, cellsnp-lite, MQuad, VarTrix, MiTo, GIFT and the GoT tools with `ds.variants.import_counts` (#119).
- Keep the informative mitochondrial variants with `informative`, by mgatk's statistics and Signac's or MAESTER's thresholds, and call clones from their frequencies with `frequency_clones` (#120).
- Call genotypes at targeted sites with `genotypes`, and the clones that mutant calls define with `genotype_clones` (#121). By default `genotype_clones` fits a likelihood model that tolerates allelic dropout: on 200,000 simulated cells it recovers the clones with an adjusted Rand index of 0.79, where the exact rule reaches 0.01 (#158).
- Read Mission Bio Tapestri DNA and protein files into a store with `cytearc.TapestriToZarr` and `cytearc.TapestriReader`, and DAb-seq files with `import_counts` (#122, #160).
- New figures: `ds.plots.variant_depth`, `variant_statistics`, `allele_frequencies` and `genotypes` (#119, #120, #121, #150).

### Trajectories, lineages and potency

- Resolve gene dynamics by lineage on a fate map with `ds.trajectory.lineage_markers`, `drivers`, `lineage_aggregation`, fate-weighted principal `curves` and a Slingshot-style `lineage_tree` (#39). Drivers match CellRank 2.3.3's correlation test on the pancreas example. New figures `ds.plots.lineage_trends`, `lineage_heatmap`, `lineage_curves` and `lineage_tree` draw from the colorblind palette (#39, #340).
- Label each cell by the lineage it follows and find where each pair of lineages parts with `ds.trajectory.lineage_membership`, and select the cells around a branch point with `branch_cells` (#246, #331).
- Return lineage curves drawn in a layout as a table with `ds.trajectory.curves_in_layout`, and build a cluster tree without a store with `cytearc.trajectory.build_cluster_tree` (#238).
- Score pseudotime and lineage trees on some of a graph's cells, such as a few clusters, with `cells=` (#243).
- Bound the pseudotime solve with `solver_tol` and `max_iterations`, follow its progress, and choose among graph components (#222). The default untruncated solve scores a million cells in about 30 s (#229).
- Direct a fate map by any per-cell score with `ds.trajectory.fate(direction=...)`, such as another tool's pseudotime, in place of a CyteArc pseudotime (#247, #341).
- Score how differentiated each cell is with `ds.scores.potency`, from its expression on a STRING protein network, by CCAT (the default) or the signaling entropy rate (#285, #288, #300). The scores match SCENT 1.1, and a potency score can direct a fate map without source cells. The human and mouse networks download on first use and are checked against their recorded digests.

### Layouts and clustering

- `ds.embeddings.localmap` lays out a connectivity map with LocalMAP, a PaCMAP extension that separates clusters that sit next to each other (#332). On 1.1 million Tabula Sapiens cells it takes 42 s on 16 CPUs, against 1,093 s for UMAP's default. The RNA, ATAC and ADT recipes add a LocalMAP layout with `localmap=True` (#335).
- `ds.clusters.connectivity` returns the graph weight between clusters as node and edge tables, without drawing a figure (#226).

### Pipeline recipes

- `ds.pipeline.plan` reports which stages of a recipe call would be reused and which computed, and why, without running anything (#227).
- `ds.pipeline.describe` lists a recipe's stage settings and their defaults, without a store (#241).
- `run.settings()` returns the settings that a run recorded, and `ds.pipeline.rerun(run, **overrides)` runs the recipe again, changing only what the call passes (#370). A rerun with a new Leiden resolution reuses every stage up to UMAP.
- Recipes refuse more settings before writing anything: a Harmony batch column that leaves a cell without a label in ADT and ATAC runs (#175), doublet scoring on an assay that is not normalized by library size (#339), and unscaled PCA with doublet scoring or an ANN metric other than `"l2"` or `"cosine"` (#344).
- Each stage records CPU time, threads, peak memory and network bytes beside the cores and memory its process had (#283).
- Applications can follow runs with `cytearc.pipeline_listener`, stop them with `cytearc.CancellationToken`, and send logs to the standard library logger with `cytearc.configure_output(stdlib=True)` (#38).

### Import, storage and data access

- `H5adToZarr`, `CrToZarr`, `CSVtoZarr`, `SparseToZarr` and `SeuratToZarr` import normalized values beside counts through `values=` (#165).
- `SparseToZarr` builds a store of several assays, such as RNA, guides and hashtags, from in-memory matrices of the same cells (#184).
- Import writers take `policy="fit"` to write the largest count layout that fits `mem_budget` (#224).
- Categorical columns are stored as integer codes beside their categories: inserted pandas Categoricals (#233), `H5adToZarr(categorical_columns=True)` (#249), grouping and pseudobulk that read the codes (#251), and exports that write AnnData categoricals (#252). A 300-label column of 600,000 cells takes 1.8 MB in place of 48.6 MB.
- `mount_datastore` takes `source_storage_options`, so a target in a private bucket can mount a public `hf://` source (#242). `mount_datastore` and `create_composite` take `relative_sources=True`, so a folder of stores keeps opening after it is moved or uploaded (#244), and `create_composite(at=...)` writes a composite to a local path, a bucket or a Zarr store (#245).
- `DataStoreMerge` and `create_composite(features="union")` warn when their sources measured different features, because the result reads zero counts for the features a source lacks (#337, #346).
- `ds.mapping.run(feature_key="names")` maps a query onto a reference by feature name, such as gene symbols onto Ensembl IDs (#236).
- `ds.artifacts.load_values` reads a cell column over a selection (#228) and leaves out the cell IDs with `cell_ids=False` (#235).
- `ds.qc.hto_demultiplexing` demultiplexes each sample with its own hashtags, through `sample_column=` or a mapping passed as `hashtags=` (#191).
- `ds.regulons.specificity` and `ds.regulons.connection_specificity` compute regulon specificity scores and the connection specificity index from stored scores (#240).

### Diagnostics and memory budgets

- Saved results record diagnostics, such as how many file barcodes matched no cell, which `ds.artifacts.inspect(ref).diagnostics` returns. Operations warn from them with `cytearc.DiagnosticWarning` when they compute a result and again when they reuse it (#148, #149, #179, #190, #195, #196, #248). The clone, character matrix and AIRR exports return an `ExportSummary` (#149).
- A memory budget too small for a step raises `cytearc.MemoryBudgetError`, whose `needed_bytes` is the smallest `mem_budget` that passes the step (#141, #142). Budgeted reads decode on the store's `nthreads` threads, so a budget holds on busy machines (#143), and import refusals state the importer's buffer apart from resident data, so a 0.56 GB matrix no longer reads as needing 13 GB (#177).

## New tutorials

- [Pooled CRISPR screens](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/crispr-screens) analyzes the ECCITE-seq screen of Papalexi et al. (2021), 20,729 THP-1 cells, from guide calls to the genes each perturbation changes (#75).
- [Immune repertoires](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/immune-repertoires) imports the TCR and BCR chains of 10,548 blood cells from one healthy donor, groups the cells into clonotypes and compares the clonal structure of five T cell types (#161).
- [Lineage tracing](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/lineage-tracing) scores a fate map against the clones of the LARRY experiment of Weinreb et al. (2020), 130,887 mouse hematopoietic cells (#162).
- [Lineage recorders](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/lineage-recorders) cuts the PEtracer phylogeny of a mouse embryo collected at E7.5 (Colgan et al. 2026) into clones every half day and measures which cell types share them (#163).
- [Mitochondrial lineage tracing](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/mitochondrial-lineage-tracing) calls clones in a colorectal tumor from mitochondrial DNA variants, on the mtscATAC-seq data of Lareau et al. (2020) (#164).
- [Lineage dynamics](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/lineage-dynamics) follows genes along the four endocrine lineages of the developing mouse pancreas (#39).
- [Lineage curves and trajectory checks](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/lineage-curves) draws one curve per pancreas lineage and checks the trajectory that the curves follow (#39, #314).
- [Fate mapping and potency](https://docs.nygen.io/CyteArc/tutorials/fate-mapping) gains a section that directs a fate map by a potency score, without source cells (#290).

## Major bug fixes

- Saved Numba kernels could return wrong numbers after an upgrade, an edit or a branch switch, because a kernel kept the old code of the kernels it calls in other files, the Leiden kernels among them. Kernels now compile again when any CyteArc kernel module or the CyteArc release changes (#77, #90).
- An RNA-class assay's stored `size_factor` was truncated to an integer, so a size factor of 0.5 became 0 and zeroed every normalized value. Melded gene scores opened as an RNA-class assay, as the 1.3.0 scATAC-seq tutorial did, were normalized by library size a second time; their TF-IDF values now pass through (#167).
- `ds.qc.hto_demultiplexing` called nearly every cell a doublet when a hashtag's background held only zeros while ambient tags reached the cells: 20,713 of 20,729 cells in the Papalexi screen. Such counts are now refused with a `ValueError` that names the remedy, such as `sample_column=` (#189).
- The PCA elbow plot drew its line one component too low (#336).
- A block stream kept the blocks it read ahead in memory after its consumer broke out, closed it or raised, until garbage collection ran; one job held about 27 GiB per pass (#260).
- Reads and listings of `hf://` stores could wait forever, and a 5xx response failed a read at once. Each attempt now times out, and timeouts and server errors are retried for up to 3 minutes (#230).
- A writable Hugging Face store read a server error as a missing key, so Zarr could write an empty group over a parent group's metadata (#284).
- Sparse and Seurat imports planned about twice the memory they hold, and refused imports that fit. A 20,000-cell Seurat import needed a 12.4 GiB budget and now needs 2.1 GiB (#265, #303).
- `ds.plots.embedding` refused to color a layout by an artifact over another selection of the same cells, such as HTO calls made before filtering (#186).
- `ds.markers.search` refused group labels that contain `/`, such as `T/NK` (#250).
- On Windows, CyteArc could not read the machine's memory and gave every machine a 6 GiB default budget (#304).
- Running `download_dataset` again replaced the store and deleted the results saved in it (#330).
- A CyteArc plot drawn as a Jupyter session's first figure turned off Matplotlib's interactive mode (#338), and in Jupyter `PlotResult.show()` could draw a figure twice (#343).
- Plots of clusterings imported from an H5AD file with `H5adReader(cluster_keys=...)` ignored the file's category order and colors (#348), and a `CategoricalScale` that set only some fields discarded a column's stored colors (#345).

## Other fixes

- `compose_results` keeps a child figure's legends unless it can redraw all of them as shared legends (#76), keeps inset axes such as a clustered matrixplot's dendrograms (#181), and no longer raises `AttributeError` on a constrained-layout figure that holds a clustered `matrixplot` (#144).
- A block stream stopped by an error or interrupt in a notebook no longer leaves process-wide Zarr I/O, BLAS or OpenMP limits in place, which had made later BLAS work run about twice as long (#126, #132).
- Reads of cell-aligned artifacts, such as `ds.artifacts.load_values` and `ds.select_cells`, charge their arrays in the order they read them, so the budgets they need fall (#182).
- `ds.plots.composition`, `cluster_connectivity` and `modality_weights` accept inputs whose cell selections hold the same cells through different artifacts (#193).
- `H5adReader` names what a malformed h5ad matrix lacks, such as an empty `X` group or a CSR group without `indptr`, and opening a metadata table that holds a 0-d array raises a `ValueError` naming the column in place of a bare `IndexError` (#374).

## Performance

- Imports of dense h5ad files plan memory from the nonzero values and write through dense row bands: the 310,385-cell K562 screen imports with the default count layout within a 3 GiB budget, in place of 115 GiB (#188, #194, #197).
- `H5adToZarr` scans a large matrix for its value ranges in several processes, about 9 times faster on 16 CPUs (#239), and encodes imported columns as whole arrays, so the cell columns of a 500,000-cell h5ad import in 1.2 s in place of 3.5 s (#224).
- Count reads run on an event loop in each reading thread, so a block stream's readers copy blocks in parallel: about twice as many cells per second from a Hugging Face composite (#267). Closing a stream early cancels its running reads (#268), and log-normalized blocks hold one array in place of two (#262).
- A read-only Hugging Face store lists its objects once and reads each key with one request: opening ten CyteBase stores takes 12 Hub API calls in place of 769, and 9 s in place of 124 s (#264).
- `create_composite` fetches metadata concurrently and reads its count pass in parallel segments, so a composite of ten CyteBase stores takes 47 s in place of about 93 s (#263, #281).
- `to_h5ad` compresses on the export's threads and runs 1.7 to 1.8 times faster (#231).
- `ds.qc.doublets` scores several samples at once, 2.1 to 2.3 times faster for 4 samples, and a serial UMAP layout lets other Python threads run (#232).
- `ds.regulons.grn` fits targets on worker processes, 2.8 times faster on 8 CPUs (#234).
- New stores chunk cell and feature columns by rows and by 16 MiB of values, which halves the memory needed to read a wide text column (#145, #183, #187). Writing text columns (#135) and checking a selection's cell IDs (#180) hold a fraction of the memory they did.

## Documentation

- The README describes what CyteArc does at atlas scale, with remote data in place and with reused results, and its capability table lists the analyses that this release adds (#384).
- Every tutorial was executed again and rewritten to open with its results and quote the numbers its outputs print (#309, #310, #311, #312, #313, #314, #315), after earlier re-executions against the rebuilt example stores (#38, #266, #352).
- Three pages merged into others, and their old addresses are gone: Expression dynamics into Pseudotime and expression dynamics and Trajectory validation into Lineage curves and trajectory checks (#314), and Pseudobulk and differential expression into Donor-level comparisons and pseudobulk (#313).
- The sidebar groups the tutorials into nine sections that follow an analysis from raw data to interpretation (#308). The site uses Nygen's shared branding and navigation (#40, #41), and the API reference shares the guide pages' header and navigation (#42). New API reference pages cover the perturbation, clones, repertoire and variants namespaces.
- The methods page compares the two potency measures on fifteen systems of known stage order (#298), the CRISPR screen documentation was checked against the code (#87, #95), and section headings carry no numbers (#305).

## Miscellaneous

Pull requests that change tests, CI, contributor instructions or internal structure, with no change that users see:

- Cover every line of the guide call import with tests (#44)
- Keep only project-specific agent instructions (#62)
- Speed up the screen tests and stop a memory test from flaking (#78)
- Give each rule of the screen figures one home, with every figure unchanged (#83)
- Share the screen operations' repeated code, and move their computation to the domain package (#84)
- Split the screen operations into one module per method family (#86)
- Test memory budgets with one set of helpers, and refresh the test shard durations (#96)
- Balance CI's test shards by the seconds of every test file (#130)
- Test memory budgets, held reads and downloads with one set of helpers (#131)
- Identify files with one digest, and mix seeds with one finaliser (#134)
- Test memory budgets by what calls do, not by what they trace (#154)
- Skip the live dataset tests when the Hugging Face host is unreachable (#174)
- Give the attempt after a stalled Hugging Face request a second to answer in its test (#237)
- Stop asking pull request descriptions to name the AI tools that helped (#270)
- Make the composite read-worker limit tests wait for the overlap they assert, now that reads run on several threads (#282)
- Stop GEO's refusals under load, a busy runner's late timeouts and the shared Hugging Face client from failing tests (#297)
- Keep offline Hugging Face tests from fetching the agent registry (#306)
- Keep saved notebook outputs valid when only comments change (#307)
- Test every reachable line, running the untested Numba kernels as Python against their references (#371)
- Remove code that no input reaches, and require what callers already guarantee (#372)

**Full changelog**: https://github.com/NygenAnalytics/CyteArc/compare/1.3.0...1.4.0

## [0.37.0] - 2026-11-18

### Changed
- **Protenix-v2 normal mode is about 2 % faster on Blackhole.** Triangle multiplication writes its gated output and
  moves the pair stream in bfp8 where a fused tail reads it, as Wormhole normal already does. Paired cold folds read
  1.7 s faster at a median of 79 s; accuracy unchanged on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set (same-seed
  structure 0.07 A apart against a 0.60 A bar, docking success 35/44 on both). `--fast` and Wormhole are unchanged.
- **RFdiffusion3 is about 2.5 % faster on Wormhole.** The diffusion transformer computes q, k and v in one projection
  and normalises and splits them into heads in one kernel. Page design 35.98 -> 35.09 s in `--fast`; designs are
  byte-identical. Blackhole is unchanged.
_releases.name: v0.37.0

_releases.body:
## [0.36.0] - 2026-11-17

### Changed
- **OpenFold3 normal mode is about 3 % faster on Wormhole.** The diffusion transformer's attention runs its key
  dimension in one chunk and carries the pair-bias mask in bf16. 512 residues 15.4 -> 15.0 s per fold; accuracy
  unchanged on 12 paired folds of the three complexes most sensitive to diffusion precision. OpenBind-0, `--fast` and
  Blackhole are unchanged.
- **RFD4 `--fast` is about 5 % faster on Wormhole.** A padded design now carries the pair stream in bfp8, as an
  unpadded one already did. A 336-token design reads 1.3 to 1.5 s faster (28.6 s before); designed-chain structure
  stays well inside the fast-mode bar on 12 paired seeds at that size and 35 at 620 tokens. Normal mode and Blackhole
  are unchanged.
_releases.name: v0.36.0

## [0.35.0] - 2026-11-17

### Changed
- **Boltz-2 is faster on Blackhole: `--fast` about 5 %, normal mode about 2 %.** In fast mode the pair LayerNorm runs
  inside triangle attention's projections; in normal mode triangle multiplication's tail runs as one fused kernel, as
  both already do on Wormhole. 512 residues: fast 0.57 s, normal 0.30 s faster per fold; accuracy unchanged on 44
  paired folds of the 11-complex test set.
- **Protenix-v2 `--fast` is about 3 % faster on Blackhole.** Triangle multiplication writes its gated output in bfp8
  for the memory-bound tail. On a 512-residue complex the chip time drops 18.3 -> 17.6 s; accuracy stays inside the
  fast-mode bar on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set.
- **Boltz-2 `--fast` is about 1 % faster on Wormhole.** The pair transition's SiLU now overlaps its matmuls. Output is
  byte-identical; 512 residues read 0.16 s faster per fold (median of 3 warm pairs), normal mode about 0.1 s.
- **Protenix-v2 normal mode is about 3 % faster on Wormhole.** Triangle multiplication hands its tail a bfp8 input and
  keeps its gate output in bfp8, and the diffusion transformer uses the attention set OpenDDE already runs. 512 residues
  49.4 -> 48.1 s per warm fold; accuracy unchanged on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set.
- **Boltz-2 normal mode is about 1 s faster on Blackhole.** The atom transformer keeps its intermediates in L1 as it
  already does on Wormhole. Output is byte-identical; 512 residues read 1.0 s faster per fold (median of 4 pairs).
- **Boltz-2 normal mode is about 18 % faster on Wormhole.** Triangle multiplication's input projection runs as one fused
  kernel and triangle attention writes its LayerNorm outputs in bfp8, both as `--fast` already does. 512 residues
  21.5 -> 17.7 s per fold (median of 4 pairs); accuracy unchanged on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set.
- **Boltz-2 normal mode is about 6 % faster on Wormhole.** Triangle multiplication's output tail runs as one fused
  kernel, as it already does in `--fast`. 512 residues read 1.3 s faster per fold (median of 4 pairs); accuracy
  unchanged on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set.

### Fixed
- **Boltz-2 on Blackhole places atoms far from the origin more precisely.** The diffusion model's attention ran at a
  lower matmul fidelity that dropped low bits of atom positions, so bond-length error grew with distance from the
  origin. It now runs at full fidelity in both modes: CA-lDDT rises slightly on the 11-complex test set, docking is
  unchanged and 512 residues fold at the same speed.
_releases.name: v0.35.0

_releases.body:
## [0.34.0] - 2026-11-16

### Changed
- **ESMFold2 is about 2 % faster on Wormhole when the MSA is no deeper than the encoder's limit.** The MSA encoder's pair
  now stays on the chip instead of a round trip through the host. Output is unchanged: 512 residues 23.3 -> 22.8 s,
  748 residues 54.9 -> 53.7 s.
- **Protenix-v2 `--fast` is about 2 % faster on Wormhole.** The pair transition's LayerNorm and residual now run inside
  its fused kernel, and triangle multiplication keeps one more intermediate in bfp8. 512 residues 42.3 -> 41.4 s;
  accuracy unchanged on 44 paired folds of the 11-complex test set.

### Fixed
- **A killed `tt-bio` command no longer leaves a stuck worker holding its card.** When `timeout` or a
  `kill` ended the CLI while a worker was stuck opening its chip, the worker kept the card until someone killed it
  by hand. It now gets SIGTERM as before and, if still alive 90 s later, SIGKILL. Embedding shards and BoltzGen
  per-chip workers are covered too.
- **One dead chip no longer stalls device opens on every other chip of the host.** Opens are serialized host-wide, so
  an open that never returned held every other chip's open behind it. A chip whose ARC firmware has stopped is now
  refused in about 2 s with an error naming the chip and its reset command, before anything is opened. A process still
  inside an open or close after 10 minutes exits and frees the host for the next open, and the check that a fresh chip
  can run a program, which once hung 57 minutes on its own card, ends after 4. A waiting open prints which process
  holds the host lock and since when.
_releases.name: v0.34.0

_releases.body:
## [0.33.0] - 2026-11-15

### Changed
- **OpenDDE reads the same reference conformers as upstream OpenDDE 1.2.0.** It used the CCD ideal coordinates,
  up to 2.8 A off in intra-residue distances for amino acids and 4.1 A for nucleotides; it now downloads OpenDDE's own
  conformer table (143 MB, once). Glycans, modified residues and cyclic peptides are also linked the way upstream
  links them. Accuracy is unchanged within seed noise on 11 complexes and 7 ligand complexes.
- **OpenDDE on Wormhole folds about 2 % faster in the default mode** (384 tokens 77.5 -> 75.9 s on a Galaxy chip at
  1000 MHz). Structures agree with the previous release to 0.11 A median on 11 complexes, well inside seed noise.
- **Jobs that share an MSA cache search each sequence once.** When several jobs in a burst need the same chain, the
  first one searches and the others wait and read its result, for every MSA model, paired and unpaired. Before, only
  Boltz-2 did this; the rest repeated the search in every job. Same search, same output.

### Fixed
- **OpenFold3 returns its coordinates in full precision.** The sampler rounded every final atom position to bfloat16,
  0.125 A at 16-32 A from the origin and 0.5 A at 64-128 A, which distorted backbone bond lengths in large complexes.
_releases.name: v0.33.0

## [0.32.0] - 2026-11-12

### Added
- **Mol-1 can be guided by what you already know about the binding.** A job that carries a `constraints` object folds
  on Molence's Mol-1-constraint weights: `site` names the residues in the binding site, `contact` the pairs that
  should touch, `exclusion` the regions to keep clear, in any combination
  ([docs/mol1.md](docs/mol1.md#guiding-a-prediction-mol-1-constraint)). The weights download on first use, and only
  for a job that names a condition; a job without one folds on the base weights exactly as before. Thanks to
  [Molence Bio](https://github.com/molence/Mol-1) for releasing the model and the weights under Apache-2.0.
_releases.name: v0.32.0

### Changed
- **Mol-1 `--fast` is faster than the default mode.** It used to drop Mol-1's tuned kernels and ran about 1.5x slower.

**PyPI:** https://pypi.org/project/omicverse/2.4.3/ · `pip install -U omicverse`

### scanpy is optional
omicverse's own code no longer imports or calls scanpy (~370 calls in 93 files). `pip install omicverse` does not install it; `pip install "omicverse[scanpy]"` (or `[full]`) does. New `ov.pp` functions with scanpy's outputs — `calculate_qc_metrics`, `score_genes`, `diffmap`, `dpt`, `draw_graph`, `dendrogram`, `subsample` — plus native `regress`, `louvain`, `score_genes_cell_cycle`, identical to scanpy 1.11.5 on SEA-AD cells (#1069).

### AnnData and AnnDataOOM
Every registered function accepts the disk-backed object from `ov.read(path, storage='disk')`: functions that need the matrix in memory read it in (after a memory check), run, and write their new results back; `ov.utils.to_memory()` gives a plain AnnData for other tools. `get_celltype_marker`, `space.svg(mode='pearsonr')` and `pl.markers_dotplot` now work on disk-backed data (#1069). `ov.read` keeps `storage='memory'` as the default (#1067, #1068).

### Fixes
- `ov.pp.umap` optimises for 500 / 200 epochs like umap-learn and scanpy (the CPU default was 10 / 20) (#1069).
- `anndataoom-fast>=0.1.6`: the UMAP layout no longer stalls on small graphs with many threads.
- `ov.pp.leiden(flavor='igraph')` matches scanpy for the same seed; CPU-only Leiden arguments work in mixed / GPU mode (#1069, #1070).
- `umap(init_pos='paga')`, `regress(layer=...)`, palettes > 28 categories, scFoundation MNN, scGPT preprocessing (#1069); `ov.pp.ambient` keeps counts sparse (#1049).

### New
- `ov.bulk.recover_sample_annotations` and helpers (#1050).
- `ov.space` marker signatures with Cell Ontology lineage markers (#1066).

### Documentation
README benchmark (SEA-AD, 1.38M cells) and feature-coverage figures, docs page *Feature coverage* (#1051–#1065); OpenClaw / MCP / J.A.R.V.I.S. docs moved to [OmicClaw](https://github.com/omicverse/omicclaw) (#1057).

Full notes: [Release notes](https://omicverse.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Release_notes/) (v 2.4.3).

### Where the matrix lives: `ov.read(path, storage=...)`
- `storage='memory'` (default) loads an AnnData into RAM; `storage='disk'` keeps the matrix on disk — AnnDataOOM in `cpu` / `cpu-gpu-mixed` mode, Dask row blocks streamed to the GPU in `gpu` mode. `backend='python'|'rust'` still works with a `FutureWarning` (#1033)

- `qc`, `preprocess`, `scale`, `pca` and COSG markers stream the matrix through the GPU, so it never has to fit in GPU or host memory; SEA-AD MTG (1.38M cells) runs on one H100 (#1033). Pinned-copy fix and 7x faster gzip reads (#1037)

- Threaded loading, subsets, normalisation and checks: SEA-AD MTG standard workflow 271 s → 75 s at 64 threads, identical results (#1046)
- `ov.pp.scale` keeps the scaled layer implicit when the dense matrix would exceed 32 GB; `ov.pp.pca` gives the same result (#1046)

- **bugfix**: serialization now fails fast when a covariance function (or a predictor) belongs to a class that could not be resolved again on loading. Mellon stores classes by name and recovers them with `getattr(import_module(module_name), classname)`, so a class that is not bound at the top level of its module — most commonly one defined inside a factory function — produced a file that `Covariance.from_dict` / `Predictor.from_json` could not load. Previously `to_json()` wrote that file without complaint and the `AttributeError` surfaced only at load time, potentially long after the fit it was meant to preserve. `to_json()` / `to_dict()` now raise a `TypeError` naming the offending qualified name and asking for a module-level definition. Module-level covariance functions, including user-defined ones, are unaffected and still round-trip exactly; existing serialized files still load. `Predictor.copy()` is deliberately not affected, as it never resolves the predictor class by name.
 - the guard above lives in `Covariance.__getstate__`, which is also Python's `copy`/`pickle` hook, so `copy.deepcopy()` and `pickle.dumps()` of such a covariance function now raise the same `TypeError`. Previously `deepcopy` succeeded, since it carries the class by reference instead of resolving it by name; `pickle` failed on its own. Only classes that were already unserializable are affected. For the same reason `Predictor.copy()` of a predictor with such a covariance function now raises `TypeError` up front instead of the previous `AttributeError` from the load path — it did not work before either.
 - composite covariance functions (`+`, `*`, `**`) now record the full module of their class instead of only the top-level package, so a user-defined `CovariancePair` subclass living in a subpackage can be resolved on loading. Files written by earlier versions continue to load unchanged.
 - `compute_d_factal` is renamed to **`compute_d_fractal`**, correcting the spelling of "fractal". The new name is the canonical one and is what `d_method="fractal"` now calls internally. **`compute_d_factal` continues to work**: it is retained as an alias that forwards to `compute_d_fractal`, is still exported from `mellon.parameters`, and remains listed in `__all__`, so existing code needs no change. **No deprecation warning is emitted** — the old name is used widely enough downstream that a warning on by default would be noise rather than signal. Callers writing new code should prefer `compute_d_fractal`.
 - **removed**: the `mellon-test` console script. It was declared as `mellon-test = "pytest:main"` while `pytest` is only a `dev` extra, so on a normal install it failed immediately with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest'`. It could not have worked even with `pytest` present: the installed distribution contains only the `mellon` package, never the test suite, and the script invoked `pytest.main()` with no arguments — so it would have collected from whatever directory it happened to be run in. Run the tests from a source checkout with `pytest` instead. **This removes a published command**, so any script invoking `mellon-test` will now get "command not found" rather than the `ModuleNotFoundError` it got before.
 - **bugfix**: declare `packaging` as a runtime dependency. `mellon.base_predictor` has imported `packaging.version` at module scope since v1.5.0, but `packaging` was never listed in the project dependencies, so installing Mellon into an environment that provided only its declared requirements failed at `import mellon` with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'packaging'`. Environments that happened to supply `packaging` transitively — including any install of the `dev` or `docs` extras — were unaffected, which is why it went unnoticed. If you have ever hit `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'packaging'` on a fresh install of Mellon, this is the fix.
 - the GP leverage diagonal `diag(B M^-1 B^T)` is now computed with a Cholesky solve instead of an explicit `jnp.linalg.inv(M)`. `M = sigma^2 K_uu + B^T B` (plus jitter) is symmetric positive definite by construction, so the inverse was never needed. All five sites are converted: `_LandmarksConditional._compute_obs_variance` and `._leverage` (scalar and per-feature sigma) and `_LandmarksConditionalCholesky._leverage`. Results are unchanged to within rounding (worst relative difference 1.8e-7 across 30 public-API comparisons; 1.9e-4 on a real 5,000-landmark problem with cond(M) = 2.5e13, where both forms agree with a QR reference to about 1e-4 and neither is uniformly the more accurate).
 - this also removes a segfault. `jnp.linalg.inv` lowers to LU (`getrf`), which dispatches to OpenBLAS's threaded `dgetrf_parallel`; at 5,000 landmarks that routine overflows the stack of the thread JAX calls it on and the process dies with SIGSEGV. Measured on OpenBLAS 0.3.30: 12/12 crashes end-to-end at `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=16` against 0/12 at 1 thread, and 6/12 against 0/12 for the unpatched and patched code run back to back (not concurrently). Affects any caller using landmarks with `obs_variance=True` or `Predictor.leverage()`. The Cholesky path uses `potrf` and is unaffected. `export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` remains a valid workaround on older versions.
 - note: with `jitter=0`, or in float32, the Cholesky form returns NaN for matrices where the old `inv` returned finite values. In every such case checked the old values were numerically meaningless (errors above 25%, leverages outside [0, 1]), so this surfaces a failure that was previously silent. The default `jitter=1e-6` in float64 — what every estimator uses — is unaffected.

_releases.body:
### Fixed

- `pt.aliphatic_index()` no longer returns a diluted number for an ambiguous residue, and `pt.molar_extinction_coefficient()` no longer assumes an unspecified residue is not a chromophore. Both counted a residue they could not place as zero while still counting it in the length, so `pt.aliphatic_index("AJILAVIL")` gave 256.25 where `AVILAVIL` gives 292.5, although `J` is leucine or isoleucine and both occupy the same aliphatic volume. An ambiguous residue is now resolved when every amino acid it stands for contributes the same amount (`J` is 3.9 for the aliphatic index, and `B`, `J` and `Z` are exact zeros for both numbers, since none of aspartate, asparagine, leucine, isoleucine, glutamate or glutamine is aliphatic or absorbs at 280 nm), and refused with `PeptacularError` when they differ. `X` stands for any amino acid, so it is always refused: its aliphatic volume is unknown, and it could be tryptophan or tyrosine. A residue outside the twenty (`U`, `O`) is a determinate zero for both, because it is a defined residue that is neither aliphatic nor a chromophore. `pt.instability_index()` is unchanged and still refuses every residue with no `DIWV` entry, which is every one of these, because no ambiguity code can be resolved there: the two amino acids a code stands for have different `DIWV` values. So the aliphatic index of a peptide holding `J` is determined while its instability index is not, and the two now say so. The published benchmark values are unchanged.

- A charge carrier error in a comma-separated list now carries the position of the carrier that is wrong. `pt.parse("EMEVEESPEK/[Na:z+1,H:z+1^0]")` reported `Position 12`, the first carrier, while the bad multiplier is in the second at `Position 19`, which is where a malformed carrier in the same list already pointed. The message also no longer writes `Invalid charge carrier` twice when the carrier parser names the carrier itself: `/[Na:Z+1]` read `Invalid charge carrier 'Na:Z+1': Invalid charge carrier 'Na:Z+1': a charge carrier must be a bare charged formula`.

- **`pt.parse` is stricter about charge carriers.** `parse` now checks the syntax of each charge carrier between `/[` and `]` with the same function that resolves it for `mass()` and `mz()`, instead of copying any text through. A string whose carrier is impossible as written used to parse and serialize, then raised `ProFormaFormatError` the first time `charge_state` or `mz()` was used; now `pt.parse` raises that error up front, naming the carrier and its position. This covers `EMEVEESPEK/[]`, `EMEVEESPEK/[garbage]` and `EMEVEESPEK/[Na:zX]`, and also a carrier whose formula cannot be read, such as `/[M+2H]` or `/[+2Na+]`. Code that parsed such a string and never asked for a mass or m/z will now get an exception. `pt.validate` returns `False` for them as before. Valid carriers (`/2`, `/-1`, `/[Na:z+1]`, `/[Na:z+1,H:z+1]`, `/[H-2Na1:z+1]`, `/[Na:z+1^2]`) parse and give the same charge states and m/z as before, and modification names (`PEP[Foo]TIDE`) are still resolved lazily. The Pyteomics and psm-utils adapters report a target library's unreadable charge text as a failed round trip, as they did before.

- `pt.fragment()`, `pt.fast_fragment()`, `pt.fragment_arrays()` and `ProFormaAnnotation.frag()` raise `UnsupportedOperationError` for a cross-linked or branched peptidoform instead of returning the ions of the linear peptide. A `#XL` or `#BRANCH` label on two residues bonds those residues to each other, so a single backbone cleavage between them does not separate the two halves and the ions at those positions do not exist: `pt.fragment("EVTK[X:DSS#XL1]LEK[#XL1]SEFD", ion_types=("b",), charges=(1,))` returned b4, b5 and b6 at 596.329, 709.413 and 838.456 as if K4 and K7 were unlinked. That bond is not modelled (ProForma 2.1 section 9.2, see `PROFORMA_COMPLIANCE.md`), and the interchain form (`//`) is already refused when parsed, so the intrachain form is now refused too and `pt.diagnose(seq, "fragment")` reports it. `mass()`, `neutral_mass()`, `mz()` and `comp()` are unchanged and still describe the intact molecule. A label on one residue only is a dead-end linker, which bonds nothing and still fragments as an ordinary modification, and a localization group such as `#g1` is not affected.
- `count_residues` and `percent_residues` count the residues inside an interval instead of counting the interval as one residue. With an interval anywhere in the sequence the counts did not sum to the sequence length: `pt.count_residues("PEP(?TI)DE")` returned a `(?TI)` key and a total of 6 for a 7-residue peptide, and `(?PEP)TIDE` totalled 5 for 7 residues, so `percent_residues` was computed over the wrong total. Now `T` and `I` are counted individually. An interval without modifications adds no key of its own. An interval with modifications is written onto each residue it spans as a one-residue interval with the same modifications, so `PEP(?TI)[Phospho]DE` holds `(?T)[Phospho]` and `(?I)[Phospho]`, which keeps the modification visible and apart from a localised `T[Phospho]`. `include_mods=False` and `split` are unchanged.
- `count_residues` and `percent_residues` write interval keys that `pt.parse` reads back when the interval meets a terminal modification or a global isotope label. The residue's whole key was wrapped in the interval's parentheses, so `[Acetyl]-(?PEP)[Phospho]TIDE` gave `(?[Acetyl]-P)[Phospho]`, `PEPTID(?E)[Phospho]-[Amidated]` gave `(?E-[Amidated])[Phospho]` and `<13C>PEP(?TI)[Phospho]DE` gave `(?<13C>T)[Phospho]`, and all three raise `ProFormaFormatError` when parsed. The parentheses now hold the residue and its own modifications only, giving `[Acetyl]-(?P)[Phospho]`, `(?E)[Phospho]-[Amidated]` and `<13C>(?T)[Phospho]`. The counts are unchanged (#113).
- `pt.count_residues()` and `pt.percent_residues()` no longer carry the parent's annotations into their keys. Counting a charged peptide used to give `{'P/2': 2, 'E/2': 2, …}` instead of `{'P': 2, 'E': 2, …}`. A labile modification gave `{+79.966}P`, an unlocalised one `[Phospho]?P`, and a name `(>Name)P`. The keys now hold the residue and the modifications localised to it, including its own N- or C-terminal modification, so `pt.count_residues("PEPTIDE/2") == pt.count_residues("PEPTIDE")`. A global isotope label stays in the key, because it applies to every residue, so `pt.count_residues("<13C>PEPTIDE")` gives `{'<13C>P': 2, …}` (#105).
- `pt.split()` no longer refuses a peptide whose localization group spans more than one residue. The guard that stops a slice cutting a group fired on the per-residue slices a split makes, so `pt.split`, `pt.count_residues`, `pt.percent_residues`, `pt.permutations`, `pt.combinations`, `pt.combinations_with_replacement`, `pt.product` and `pt.sort` all raised `PeptacularError` on valid ProForma such as `PEPT[Phospho#g1]IDEK[#g1]`. A split keeps every position, so every member of the group is still present across the pieces and `pt.join(pt.split(seq))` returns the original, scores included. A partial slice, a digest or a coverage comparison that would cut a group still raises.
- Slicing or digesting an annotation whose localization group (a primary tag plus `#label` references) would be split between the slice and the rest now raises `PeptacularError` naming the group, instead of silently dropping the modification or leaving a dangling `#label` reference. A group wholly inside the slice is unchanged.
- `averagine_comp` no longer rounds each element on its own. It keeps the integer compositions within 1 Da of the requested monoisotopic mass and returns the one whose isotope envelope best matches the fractional averagine envelope. Independent rounding put `pt.averagine_comp(1000.0)` at 978.5134 Da, 21.49 Da short; it now lands within 0.5 Da. Element counts stay non-negative integers within 2 of `estimate_averagine_comp`.
- ProForma JSON non-finite-number errors consistently include the rejected value (`nan`, `inf`, or `-inf`) when encoding objects, decoding mappings, or parsing JSON constants.
- `pt.iter_batch()` and every function that takes `n_workers` or `chunksize` name the rejected value in the message instead of only the parameter. `pt.iter_batch("mass", sequences, errors="bogus")` said `errors must be 'raise' or 'collect'` and now says `errors must be 'raise' or 'collect', got 'bogus'`; `batch_size=0` says `batch_size must be a positive integer, got 0`. The validator is shared with the parallel helpers, so `pt.mass(sequences, n_workers=0)` reads `n_workers must be a positive integer, got 0` (#81).
- ProForma JSON type errors name the type they received. `pt.from_proforma_dict` on a document whose `sequence` is a number said `sequence must have type str | None` and now says `sequence must have type str | None, got int`. The same holds for the object checks (`names and modifications must be JSON objects, got names int and modifications dict`), the array check (`modifications.internal must be an array or null, got int`) and the modification-count check (`N-terminal modifications must map modification strings to integer counts, got str -> str`) (#80).
- `pt.fragment()`, `pt.fast_fragment()`, `pt.fragment_arrays()` and `ProFormaAnnotation.frag()` return the internal and satellite ions of a peptide whose localization group spans more than one residue, instead of raising `PeptacularError`. The guard that refuses a slice cutting a localization group fired on the per-ion slices the fragment engine makes, so `pt.fragment("PEPT[Phospho#g1]IDEK[#g1]", ion_types=("i",), charges=(1,))` raised `Localization group #g1 would be cut by slice [3:4]` where 5.1.0 gave 8 immonium ions. It affected the immonium, by, ay, w, d and v series and `fragment_arrays`, while a, b, c, x, y, z, the precursor and `fast_fragment` were unaffected. The engine's slices now carry the same exemption that a split has had since #113, because taking a peptide apart ion by ion divides a group between the pieces rather than losing it. The ions and their m/z are what 5.1.0 returned, to the last digit, for all thirteen ion types. Slicing an annotation across a group, and digesting or comparing coverage in a way that would cut one, still raise.
- `pt.averagine_comp()` and `pt.estimate_isotopic_distribution()` return a composition for a mass too small to show six isotope peaks, instead of raising `ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1`. A candidate that small has fewer envelope peaks than the fractional reference it is compared against, and the comparison required equal lengths: `pt.averagine_comp(18.0106)` raised where 5.1.0 gave `{H: 2, O: 1}`, and 74 of the 128 masses on a quarter-dalton grid up to 32 Da were affected, none above. A peak the composition cannot produce now counts as the zero abundance it is, and a candidate carrying a peak the envelope does not have is rejected rather than compared. Compositions at every mass on that grid match 5.1.0, and masses above it are unchanged.
- `pt.fragmentation_preset(method, charge_state=...)` keeps the sign of the precursor charge. It took the magnitude, so `charge_state=-3` asked for charges 1 and 2 of a peptide carrying -3 and `pt.fragment("PEPTIDEK/-3", **pt.fragmentation_preset("cid", charge_state=-3))` returned the positive ions of a negative precursor, where the same call without the preset gives -2 and -1. `-3` now gives `charges=(-2, -1)` and `3` still gives `(1, 2)`: one charge per magnitude from 1 to `max(1, abs(charge_state) - 1)`, each with the sign of `charge_state`. The presets themselves are unchanged.
- `ProFormaAnnotation.to_ip2()` and `ProFormaAnnotation.to_diann()` raise `PeptacularError` instead of writing a terminal modification whose name holds a square bracket, such as `Formula:[13C2]H3`. Both readers find a terminal group with a bracket pattern that stops at the first `]`, so the written string either did not parse or parsed as something else: `pt.parse("EEN[Formula:[13C2]H3]-[UNIMOD:35]").to_ip2()` read back as `EEN[Formula:[13C2]H3][UNIMOD:35]`, moving the C-terminal modification onto the residue with no error, and `pt.parse("PEPTIDE-[Formula:[13C2]H3]").to_diann()` wrote a string `from_diann` rejects. `to_ip2` also refuses a C-terminal modification written after a last residue whose own name holds a bracket, which is the same ambiguity one position along. An internal modification name is read back unchanged and is still written, and so is every terminal name without a bracket.

### Changed

- `pt.averagine_comp()` caches its composition search per mass (`functools.lru_cache`, at most 1024 masses), so repeated calls with the same mass search once, and `pt.estimate_isotopic_distribution()`, which calls it on every call, no longer pays the search again. The cache holds an immutable tuple and every call returns a new `Counter`, so editing a returned composition cannot change what the next caller gets. Returned compositions are unchanged, including the 93.38% worst k=1..5 envelope error over the envelope test peptides. A mass that is new to the cache costs the same as before. The timings that measure the win are in the pull request (#107).
- Speed up `pt.coverage()`, `pt.percent_coverage()` and `find_indices()` on unmodified sequences by using `str.find` and direct slice assignment instead of regex matching and annotation slicing. The work it stops doing is one annotation slice per match: counting the calls on a 1600-residue protein with 444 tryptic peptides gives 3076 slices before this change and none after, for the same coverage vector. The coverage vector is unchanged for every combination of `accumulate`, `ignore_mods` and `ignore_ambiguity` on plain sequences, a modified protein, modified peptides, repeated and overlapping matches and ambiguous intervals, with the one exception in the next entry. The timings that measure the win are in the pull request (#86).
- `pt.coverage()`, `pt.percent_coverage()`, `pt.find_subsequence_indices()` and `pt.is_subsequence()` called with `ignore_mods=True` now return a result where they used to raise `PeptacularError`, when the protein holds an interval or a localization group that the match's slice would cut. The old path sliced the parent once per match even though the caller had asked for modifications to be ignored, and that slice refused the cut, so `pt.coverage("PE(PT)IDE", ["PEP"], ignore_mods=True)` raised instead of returning `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]`. With `ignore_mods=False` the slice still runs and still refuses, which is what keeps the refusal meaningful (#86).

### Added

- Add ProtParam property calculations `pt.instability_index()`, `pt.aliphatic_index()` and `pt.molar_extinction_coefficient()` across `property/core.py`, `AnnotationProperties` and `sequence/properties.py`, with support for single sequences, `ProFormaAnnotation` instances, and lists with parallel execution (#114).
- `pt.fragmentation_preset(method, charge_state=...)` returns the `pt.fragment()` keyword arguments for an activation method, so naming the method replaces writing the ion series, the neutral losses and the charge rule by hand: `pt.fragment(seq, **pt.fragmentation_preset("hcd", charge_state=2))`. Seven presets, each with the primary literature it rests on: `cid` and `hcd` (b, y), `etd` and `ecd` (c, z.), `ethcd` (b, y, c, z.), `ead` (a, b, c, x, y, z.) and `uvpd` (a, b, c, x, y, z), with water and ammonia losses (water only for `uvpd`) and at most one loss per ion. `charge_state=z` sets `charges=(1, ..., max(1, z - 1))`, the same rule in every preset. `etd` carries no b or y series, because the b and y ions of an electron-transfer experiment come from collisional activation of the charge-reduced survivor, which is what `ethcd` is for. The table is public and writable as `pt.FRAGMENTATION_PRESETS` and the citations are `pt.FRAGMENTATION_PRESET_CITATIONS`. Each method has one spelling, matched without regard to case or surrounding spaces, and an instrument's own name for a method (PASEF, ETciD) is mapped to a preset by whatever reads the file. A preset is a default and not a measurement: it names the series a method usually gives, and the real series depend on the instrument, the activation energy and the peptide, so the returned dict is a fresh copy and the caller's key wins when one is overridden. An unknown method raises `PeptacularError` naming the valid names. `fast_fragment()` takes three of the four keys, so filter the preset before splatting it there.
- `ProFormaAnnotation.to_maxquant()`, `ProFormaAnnotation.from_maxquant()` and `pt.convert_maxquant_sequence()` read and write MaxQuant modified sequences, the `Modified sequence` column of `evidence.txt` and `msms.txt`. The sequence is enclosed in underscores and each modification is written in round brackets after its residue, so `[ac]-SM[ox]K` becomes `_(ac)SM(ox)K_` and `PEP[Phospho]TIDE-[Amidated]` becomes `_PEP(Phospho)TIDE(Amidated)_`. The reader matches nested parentheses, so full names such as `_ALTDM(Oxidation (M))PQM(Oxidation (M))R_` read as `ALTDM[Oxidation (M)]PQM[Oxidation (M)]R`; a leading group is N-terminal, a group after the last residue is C-terminal and every other group sits on the residue before it. `to_maxquant()` copies modification strings through unchanged and raises `PeptacularError` for isotope labels, labile modifications, unknown-position modifications, intervals, charge or charge adducts, modification multipliers, more than one modification at a terminus or on one residue, a modification on the last residue (it would be read back as a C-terminal modification) and a modification name with unbalanced parentheses.
- `ProFormaAnnotation.to_diann()` writes an annotation as a DIA-NN sequence instead of raising `NotImplementedError`. The sequence is enclosed in underscores, internal modifications are written in square brackets after the residue they sit on, N-terminal modifications are written inside the leading underscore, and C-terminal modifications trail after the closing underscore, so `[Acetyl]-PEP[Phospho]TIDE-[Amidated]` becomes `_[Acetyl]PEP[Phospho]TIDE_[Amidated]`. Modification strings are copied through unchanged; reading the result with `from_diann` gives back an equal annotation. It raises `PeptacularError` for what DIA-NN cannot express: isotope labels, labile modifications, unknown-position modifications, intervals, charge and charge adducts, or modification multipliers. It also refuses two cases that `from_diann` would not read back at all, because the reader gives only the leading bracket group a dash and rewrites only a single trailing group: more than one N-terminal modification, which would be written as `_[Acetyl][Phospho]PEPTIDE_`, and more than one C-terminal modification, which would be written as `_PEPTIDE_[Amidated][Phospho]`. Both of those strings raise `ProFormaFormatError` when read.
- `ProFormaAnnotation.to_casanovo()` writes an annotation as a Casanovo sequence string instead of raising `NotImplementedError`. Casanovo writes modifications as signed delta masses with no brackets directly after the modified residue, and N-terminal modifications as signed delta masses at the very start of the string, so `[+42.011]-PEPM[+15.995]IDEC[+57.021]` becomes `+42.011PEPM+15.995IDEC+57.021`. The delta mass number is copied through unchanged; reading the result with `from_casanovo` gives back an equal annotation. It raises `PeptacularError` for what Casanovo cannot express: modifications that are not signed delta masses, multiple modifications on one residue, multiple N-terminal modifications, C-terminal modifications, isotope labels, labile modifications, unknown-position modifications, intervals, charge or charge adducts, or modification multipliers.
- `ProFormaAnnotation.to_ip2()` writes an annotation as an IP2 sequence instead of raising `NotImplementedError`. Each modification goes in parentheses directly after its residue, N-terminal modifications lead as parenthesis groups, and C-terminal modifications trail after the last residue's own modification, so `PEPTIDE[Phospho]-[Amidated]` becomes `PEPTIDE(Phospho)(Amidated)`. The modification string is copied unchanged and no flanking residues are written; reading the result with `from_ip2_sequence` gives back an equal annotation. It raises `PeptacularError` for what IP2 cannot place: isotope labels, labile modifications, unknown-position modifications, intervals, charge and charge adducts, and a C-terminal modification on a last residue with no modification of its own. It also refuses two cases that `from_ip2_sequence` would read back differently: more than one modification on the last residue, which the reader would split into residue and C-terminal modifications, and a modification name containing parentheses.

### Documentation

- `PROFORMA_COMPLIANCE.md` says which digest `diagnose(sequence, "digest")` checks. The operation runs `ProFormaAnnotation.digest_spans`, which locates the cut sites without building the peptides, so it reports success for a sequence whose peptides `pt.digest` refuses to build: `diagnose("PRT(ESFRMS)[+19.0523]ISK", "digest", enzyme="trypsin")` returns `None` while `pt.digest` on that sequence raises `PeptacularError: Interval [3:9] would be cut by slice [2:7]`. `docs/streaming.rst` already said the batch `digest` operation returns spans rather than `pt.digest` pairs, and the compliance file sent readers to `diagnose` without that caveat.
- Add a runnable localization example to the examples gallery.
- Add executable examples for all 17 amino-acid property scale functions.
